newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead at 8.1 percent over Dole - Reuter poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead at 8.1 percent over Dole - Reuter poll.

text.p: President Clinton bounced back slightly in the latest Reuters tracking poll Wednesday to lead Republican Bob Dole by 8.1 percent, but the race for Congress continued to be a squeaker.

The survey, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby Group International, had narrowed Clinton's lead dramatically in recent days, with Tuesday's results showing the Democratic president just 5.3 percentage points ahead of Dole.

But that lead has widened again. The latest poll reported Clinton at 44.7 percent, Dole at 36.6 percent, Reform Party candidate Ross Perot 4.4 percent, other candidates at 2.1 percent and 12.2 percent undecided.
"It's hard to read anything into a single day's results, when nothing spectacular happened in terms of world peace or on the domestic front," said pollster John Zogby.
"This simply suggests to me that this is a high single digit race," he said. "There's a greater comfort level among Republicans for Dole than before, and that's still happening."

The poll was a rolling three day average of results from about 300 interviews a day, Sunday through Tuesday. The Reuters/Zogby poll of approximately 900 likely voters had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.
Daily tracking polls can show sharp fluctuations due to the relatively small sample of voters polled each day. Their value lies in tracking the trend over a period of several days.
The Reuters/Zogby tracking poll showed Clinton ahead by 20 points last week, but Dole steadily narrowed the gap over the weekend.

The Republican's best day was Monday, the day after his first presidential debate with Clinton in Hartford Connecticut, Zogby said. But by Tuesday, Clinton had widenened his lead again to 12.3 percent on that day alone.
According to the poll, Clinton's lead among Catholics was big and he continued to hold leads among all age groups and in all regions except the South.

Dole had a strong lead among born-again Christians, and he continued to receive about three in four of Republican voters and two in three of the people who think the country is on the "wrong track," Zogby said.

The gender gap between the candidates continued, with Clinton and Dole nearly tied among men (41.2 percent Clinton, 39.6 percent Dole), but Clinton was 14 points ahead among women, 47.9 percent to 33.7 percent.

Meanwhile the race for control of the next Congress could hardly be tighter. The poll said 36.4 percent plan to vote for the Republican in their district, while 36.1 percent intend to choose the Democrat.
By small margins, those polled preferred Republicans to keep the majority in both houses of Congress.
